newsitem.title: FRANCE: Channel Tunnel truck train on fire, 34 injured.
newsitem.headline: Channel Tunnel truck train on fire, 34 injured.

text.p: Firefighters from France and Britain battled a fire early on Tuesday aboard a truck shuttle train deep inside the Channel Tunnel undersea rail link in which 34 people were reported injured, two of them seriously.
The blaze, the first major incident since the tunnel opened between Britain and France two years ago, started on Monday night in a truck carrying a cargo of polystyrene.
A civic official in the French port of Calais said a total of 34 people were involved in the incident, including crew aboard the train.
He said the two most seriously injured people were taken to hospital in the larger French city of Lille, inland from the Channel. Their lives were not in danger, he said.
Six other people were taken to hospital in Calais and 26 were given first aid for varying degrees of smoke inhalation.
A spokeswoman for channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel said: "The train is still on fire. It is being tackled by both the French and British fire fighting services,"

The 35-mile (51-km) long tunnnel linking England and France was closed after the strickened freight-shuttle train, used to transport trucks and their drivers, was halted and evacuated between 9 and 10 p.m. (same GMT). It was believed to be about 12 miles (19 km) from the French end of the tunnel.
The fire broke out towards the back of the 730 metre (yard) long train, which can carry up to 28 large trucks, the Eurotunnel spokeswoman said.
"It is the first time the tunnel has been closed for an emergency. We have had safety drills in the past but this is the first real event," she said.
The passengers and crew were evacuated from the northbound tunnel to a central service shaft and then transported via another shuttle train back to France via the southbound tunnel.
More than 20 fire appliances gathered at the British end of the tunnel near Folkestone and up to six French fire engines were reported at Calais.
Crews in breathing gear were reported to be rotating in shifts to tackle the dense smoke and searing heat generated by the fire in the narrow confines of the tunnel.
Firefighters used a freshwater main running the length of the tunnel to douse the flames.

Eurotunnel said it did not know when the tunnel would be opened for passenger traffic. "We do not know exactly what damage has been caused because the firefighters are still dealing with it," the spokeswoman said.
